source_text: I. Illuxit dies victoriae illorum, et processerunt de carcere in amphitheatrum, quasi in coelum, hilares, vultu decori; si forte, gaudio paventes, non timore. Sequebatur Perpetua placido vultu et pedum incessu, ut matrona Christi Dei dilecta: vigorem oculorum suorum dejiciens ab omnium conspectu. Item Felicitas salvam se peperisse gaudens, ut ad bestias pugnaret, a sanguine, ab obstetrice ad retiarium, lotura post partum baptismo secundo. Et cum delati essent in portam, et cogerentur habitum induere i viri quidem sacerdotum Saturni, feminae vero sacratarum Cereri: generosa illa in finem usque constantia repugnavit. Dicebat enim: « Ideo ad hoc sponte pervenimus; ne libertas nostra obduceretur. Ideo animas nostras addiximus, ne tale aliquid faceremus: hoc vobiscum pacti sumus. » Agnovit injustitia justitiam: concessit tribunus, ut quomodo erant, simpliciter inducerentur. Perpetua psallebat, caput jam Aegyptii calcans. Revocatus, et Saturninus, et Saturus populo spectanti comminabantur de hoc. Ut sub conspectu Hilariani pervenerunt, gestu et nutu coeperunt Hilariano dicere: « Tu nos, inquiunt, te autem Deus judicabit. » Ad hoc populus exasperatus, flagellis eos vexari pro ordine venatorum postulavit. Et utique illi gratulati sunt, quod aliquid et de Dominicis passionibus essent consecuti. II. Sed qui dixerat: Petite et accipietis , petentibus dedit eum exitum quem quisque desideraverat. Nam, si quando inter se de martyrii sui voto sermocinabantur, Saturninus quidem omnibus bestiis velle se objici profitebatur, ut scilicet gloriosiorem gestaret coronam. Itaque in commissione spectaculi, ipse et Revocatus leopardum experti, etiam super pulpitum ab urso vexati sunt. Saturus autem nihil magis quam ursum abominabatur: sed uno morsu leopardi confici se jam praesumebat. Itaque, cum aper subministraretur, venator potius qui illum aprum subministraverat, subfossus ab eadem bestia, post dies muneris obiit. Saturus solummodo tractus est. Et cum ad ursum substrictus esset in ponte, ursus de cavea prodire noluit. Itaque secundo Saturus illaesus revocatur. III. Puellis autem ferocissimam vaccam, ideoque praeter consuetudinem comparatam, diabolus praeparavit: sexui earum etiam de bestia aemulatus. Itaque despoliatae et reticulis indutae producebantur. Horruit populus, alteram respiciens puellam delicatam, alteram a partu recenti stillantibus mammis. Ita revocatae discinguntur. Inducitur prior Perpetua; jactata est, et concidit in lumbos: et ut conspexit tunicam a latere discissam, ad velamentum femorum adduxit, pudoris potius memor, quam doloris. Dehinc requisita, et dispersos capillos infibulavit: non enim decebat martyrem dispersis capillis pati, ne in sua gloria plangere videretur. Ita surrexit; et elisam Felicitatem cum vidisset, accessit, et manum ei tradidit, et sublevavit illam. Et ambae pariter steterunt, et, populi duritia devicta, revocatae sunt in portam Sanavivariam. Illic Perpetua a quodam tunc catechumino, Rustico nomine, qui ei adhaerebat, suscepta, et quasi a somno expergita, adeo in spiritu et in ecstasi fuerat, circumspicere coepit, et stupentibus omnibus ait: « Quando, inquit, producimur ad vaccam illam nescio. » Et cum audisset quod jam evenerat, non prius credidit, nisi quasdam notas vexationis in corpore et habitu suo recognovisset, et illum catechuminum. Exinde accersitum fratrem suum, et illum catechuminum allocuta est eos, dicens: « In fide state, et invicem omnes diligites; et passionibus nostris ne scandalizemini. » IV. Idem Saturus in alia porta militem Pudentem exhortabatur dicens: « Adsum certe, sicut promisi et praedixi; nullam usque adhuc bestiam sensi. Et nunc de toto corde credas. Ecce prodeo illo, et ab uno morsu leopardi consumar. » Et statim in fine spectaculi, leopardo objectus, de uno morsu ejus tanto perfusus est sanguine, ut populus revertenti illi secundi baptismatis testimonium reclamaverit: « Salvum lotum, salvum lotum. » Plane utique salvus erat, qui hoc spectaculo claruerat. Tunc Pudenti militi: « Vale, inquit, et memor esto fidei meae; et haec te non conturbent, sed confirment. » Simulque ansulam de digito ejus petiit, et vulneri suo mersam reddidit ei, haereditatem pignoris relinquens illi, et memoriam sanguinis. Exinde jam exanimis prosternitur cum caeteris ad jugulationem solito loco. Et cum populus illos in medium postularet, ut, gladio penetrante in eorum corpore, oculos suos comites homicidii adjungeret, ultro surrexerunt et se quo volebat populus transtulerunt: ante jam osculati invicem, ut martyrium per solemnia pacis consummarent. Caeteri quidem immobiles et cum silentio ferrum receperunt: multo magis Saturus, qui et prior scalam ascenderat, prior reddidit spiritum; nam et Perpetuam sustinebat. Perpetua autem, ut aliquid doloris gustaret, inter costas puncta exululavit; et errantem dexteram tirunculi gladiatoris ipsa in jugulum suum posuit. Fortasse tanta femina aliter non potuisset occidi, quia ab immundo spiritu timebatur, nisi ipsa voluisset.
pass_a_gloss: The day of their victory shone forth, and they proceeded from the prison into the amphitheater, as if into heaven, cheerful, with a decorous face; perhaps, trembling with joy, not with fear. Perpetua was following with a placid face and a step of feet, as a matron of Christ God, beloved, casting down the vigor of her eyes from the sight of all. Also Felicity, rejoicing that she had given birth safely, so that she might fight with the beasts, from blood, from midwife to net-maker, about to be washed after childbirth with a second baptism. And when they had been led to the gate, and were being forced to put on the dress of the men indeed of the priests of Saturn, of the women truly of the consecrated of Ceres: that noble constancy resisted to the end. For she was saying: 'We came to this of our own accord; lest our liberty be obscured. We pledged our souls, lest we do such a thing: we made a pact with you about this.' Injustice recognized justice: the tribune conceded, that they be led in just as they were, simply. Perpetua was singing psalms, now trampling the head of the Egyptian. Revocatus, and Saturninus, and Saturus, threatening to the people watching, concerning this. As they came into the sight of Hilarianus, with a gesture and a nod they began to say to Hilarianus: 'You, we say, God will judge.' The people, exasperated at this, demanded that they be scourged with whips, according to the order of the hunters. And indeed they congratulated themselves, that they had attained something of the Lord's passions. But he who said: 'Ask and you will receive', gave to those asking the exit which each one desired. For when at some time they were discussing among themselves the vow of their martyrdom, Saturninus was indeed professing that he wanted to be thrown to all the beasts, so that he might carry a more glorious crown. And so, in the contest of the spectacle, he and Revocatus, having experienced the leopard, were also torn by the bear on the platform. Saturus, however, was abominating nothing more than the bear: but he was presuming that he would be finished off by one bite of the leopard. And so, when the boar was being led in, the hunter who had led in the boar, was pierced by the same beast, and died after some days of the show. Saturus alone was dragged. And when he was bound to the bear on the bridge, the bear did not want to come out of its cage. And so, Saturus, unharmed, was recalled a second time. To the girls, however, the devil prepared a most ferocious cow, and for this reason, contrary to custom, it was procured: even emulating their sex in the beast. And so, stripped and dressed in nets, they were led out. The people shuddered, looking at one girl delicate, the other with breasts dripping from recent childbirth. And so, recalled, they were stripped. Perpetua was led in first; she was thrown and fell on her loins: and when she saw that her tunic was torn on the side, she drew it to the veil of her thighs, mindful of modesty rather than pain. Then, requested, and with her hair disheveled, she bound it up: for it was not fitting for a martyr to suffer with disheveled hair, lest she seem to be lamenting in her glory. And so she arose; and seeing Felicity, bruised, she approached, and gave her her hand, and lifted her up. And both stood equally, and, the hardness of the people having been overcome, they were recalled to the Sanavivarian gate. There Perpetua, received by a certain catechumen then, Rusticus by name, who was clinging to her, and as if awakened from sleep, was so in spirit and in ecstasy, that she began to look around, and to the amazement of all said: 'When, she said, we are led out to that cow, I do not know.' And when she heard that it had already happened, she did not believe before she recognized certain signs of torment on her body and her dress, and that catechumen. Then, having summoned her brother, and having spoken to that catechumen, she said to them: 'Stand in faith, and love each other; and do not be scandalized by our passions.' The same Saturus, in another gate, was exhorting the soldier Pudens, saying: 'I am present, certainly, as I promised and predicted; I have not yet felt any beast. And now, with all my heart, believe. Behold, I proceed to that one, and I will be consumed by one bite of the leopard.' And immediately, at the end of the spectacle, having been thrown to the leopard, he was so drenched with its blood from one bite, that the people, as he returned, cried out in testimony of a second baptism: 'Washed saved, washed saved.' Clearly, he was saved, who had become famous in this spectacle. Then to the soldier Pudens: 'Farewell', he said, 'and remember my faith; and let these things not disturb you, but confirm you.' And at the same time, he asked for a ring from his finger, and having dipped it in his wound, he returned it to him, leaving to him the pledge of a guarantee, and the memory of blood. Then, already lifeless, he fell with the others to the slaughter, in the usual place. And when the people demanded that they be brought out into the middle, so that, with the sword penetrating their body, they might join their eyes to the companions of the homicide, they arose of their own accord, and transferred themselves where the people wanted: having already kissed each other, so that they might consummate the martyrdom through the solemnities of peace. The others, indeed, received the sword, immobile and in silence: much more so Saturus, who also first ascended the ladder, first gave back his spirit; for he was also supporting Perpetua. Perpetua, however, so that she might taste some pain, cried out, pierced between the ribs; and the erring right hand of the gladiatorial boy, she herself placed on her throat. Perhaps, such a woman could not have been killed otherwise, because she was feared by the unclean spirit, unless she herself had willed it.

pass_b_english: The day of their victory dawned, and they walked from the prison into the amphitheater as if entering heaven, cheerful and composed; if they trembled, it was with joy, not fear. Perpetua followed with a calm face and steady step, like a noblewoman of Christ, beloved of God, lowering her eyes from the gaze of the crowd. Felicity rejoiced that she had given birth safely, so that she might fight the beasts; from blood and the midwife to the net-fighter, she was about to be washed after childbirth with a second baptism. When they were brought to the gate and forced to put on the robes of the priests of Saturn for the men and the vestments of the consecrated of Ceres for the women, that noble constancy resisted to the end. She said: "We came here of our own free will so that our freedom would not be obscured. We pledged our souls so that we would not do such a thing; this was our agreement with you." Injustice recognized justice, and the tribune conceded that they be led in just as they were, simply dressed. Perpetua sang psalms, now treading on the head of the Egyptian. Revocatus, Saturninus, and Saturus threatened the watching crowd about this. When they came into Hilarianus's sight, they gestured and nodded to him: "You will judge us, but God will judge you." The people, enraged, demanded they be scourged according to the order of the hunters. And indeed they rejoiced that they had attained a share in the Lord's sufferings.

But he who said, "Ask and you will receive" (Matt 7:7; Luke 11:9), gave to those who asked the exit each one desired. When they discussed the vow of their martyrdom, Saturninus professed he wanted to be thrown to all the beasts, so that he might win a more glorious crown. In the contest of the spectacle, he and Revocatus faced the leopard and were also torn by the bear on the platform. Saturus, however, dreaded nothing more than the bear; he expected to be finished by a single bite of the leopard. When a boar was provided, the hunter who had brought it was gored by the same beast and died after some days of the games. Saturus alone was dragged out. When he was bound to the bear on the bridge, the bear refused to leave its cage. So Saturus was recalled a second time, unharmed.

For the women, the devil prepared a most ferocious cow, procured contrary to custom, even emulating their sex in the beast. Stripped and dressed in nets, they were led out. The people shuddered at the sight of one young woman, delicate, and the other with breasts dripping from recent childbirth. So they were recalled and allowed to dress again. Perpetua was led in first; she was thrown and fell on her loins. Seeing her tunic torn at the side, she drew it over her thighs, mindful of modesty rather than pain. Then, asked to do so, she pinned up her disheveled hair, for it was not fitting for a martyr to suffer with hair unbound, lest she appear to be lamenting in her glory. She rose, and seeing Felicity bruised, she went to her, gave her hand, and lifted her up. Both stood together, and when the people's hostility was overcome, they were recalled to the Gate of Life. There Perpetua was received by a catechumen named Rusticus, who clung to her. As if awakened from sleep — so deeply was she in spirit and ecstasy — she looked around and said to everyone's amazement: "When are we led out to that cow? I do not know." When she heard it had already happened, she would not believe until she recognized the marks of torment on her body and clothing, and saw the catechumen. Then she summoned her brother and spoke to the catechumen: "Stand firm in faith, love one another, and do not be scandalized by our sufferings."

At another gate, Saturus encouraged the soldier Pudens: "I am here, just as I promised and predicted; I have not yet felt any beast. Now believe with all your heart. See, I go to that one and will be consumed by a single bite of the leopard." Immediately at the end of the spectacle, he was thrown to the leopard and so drenched in blood from one bite that the crowd, as he returned, cried out as a testimony to a second baptism: "Washed and saved, washed and saved." Truly he was saved, who had been glorified in this spectacle. Then to Pudens he said: "Farewell, and remember my faith; let these things not disturb you but confirm you." At the same time he asked for a ring from Pudens's finger, dipped it in his wound, and returned it, leaving a pledge of his guarantee and a memory of his blood. Then, lifeless, he fell with the others to the slaughter in the usual place. When the people demanded they be brought into the middle so that, with the sword piercing their bodies, their eyes might join the spectators as companions of the homicide, they rose of their own accord and went where the people wanted. They had already kissed one another, so as to consummate their martyrdom through the solemnities of peace. The others received the sword immobile and in silence; even more so Saturus, who had also ascended the ladder first, gave up his spirit first, for he was also supporting Perpetua. Perpetua, however, so that she might taste some pain, cried out when pierced between the ribs, and herself placed the trembling right hand of the young gladiator on her throat. Perhaps such a woman could not have been killed otherwise, because she was feared by the unclean spirit, unless she herself had willed it.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text across all four sections. Scripture citations (Matt 7:7; Luke 11:9) were correctly added to the Pass B text to identify the allusion 'Petite et accipietis'. The translation of 'Sanavivariam' as 'Gate of Life' is a standard interpretive rendering of the proper name. All nuances regarding agency (e.g., 'unless she herself had willed it') and modality are preserved.

The translation accurately reflects the source text, with appropriate citations and adherence to the original meaning. The title names the thought, not just a locus. No OCR damage or uncertain readings are noted.
